bull.b: Arm’s licensing and royalty model supports exceptional gross margins while generating substantial operating and free cash flow. This combination gives the company resources to fund research, expand its ecosystem, and pursue new silicon opportunities without relying heavily on external financing.

Accelerating adoption in data centers and AI infrastructure broadens Arm beyond its established mobile base. Strong royalty growth and rising AGI CPU demand can create durable expansion as cloud providers seek energy-efficient compute for increasingly intensive workloads.

A broad installed base, large developer community, and adoption by leading cloud platforms reinforce Arm’s position as a semiconductor computing standard. The ecosystem lowers customer development barriers and supports recurring licensing and royalty opportunities across multiple end markets.

bear.b: Smartphones remain an important royalty market, so weaker handset conditions can temper near-term volume growth across Arm’s established base. This creates a durable exposure to end-market cycles even as data-center and AI demand provide newer sources of expansion.

bear.t: Supply constraints limit AGI CPU scaling
bear.b: Demand exceeding expectations does not immediately translate into revenue when production inputs and testing capacity are constrained. Persistent supply bottlenecks could delay customer deployments, limit the pace of silicon growth, and defer the broader upside from Arm’s new product strategy.

Moving from pure IP toward production silicon introduces a lower-margin phase than Arm’s traditional licensing economics. Until scale, product mix, and execution improve, AGI CPU growth could dilute consolidated profitability and require sustained investment before reaching targeted margins.
